column1: By what gestational age should a pregnant woman be offered her first routine antenatal (booking) appointment with a midwife?
column2: By $10^{+0}$ weeks of pregnancy.

column1: How many routine antenatal appointments are planned for a nulliparous woman compared to a parous woman in uncomplicated pregnancies?
column2: 10 routine appointments for nulliparous women; 7 routine appointments for parous women.

column1: What is the recommended total gestational weight gain for a woman with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI ($18.5\text{--}24.9\text{ kg/m}^2$)?
column2: $11\text{--}16\text{ kg}$

column1: What is the recommended total gestational weight gain for an overweight pregnant woman (BMI $25.0\text{--}29.9\text{ kg/m}^2$)?
column2: $7\text{--}11\text{ kg}$

column1: What is the recommended total gestational weight gain for an obese pregnant woman (BMI $\ge 30\text{ kg/m}^2$)?
column2: $5\text{--}9\text{ kg}$

column1: What haemoglobin (Hb) threshold defines anaemia during the first trimester of pregnancy?
column2: $\text{Hb} < 110\text{ g/L}$

column1: What haemoglobin (Hb) threshold defines anaemia during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy?
column2: $\text{Hb} < 105\text{ g/L}$

column1: What haemoglobin (Hb) threshold defines anaemia in the postpartum period?
column2: $\text{Hb} < 100\text{ g/L}$

column1: At what gestational period does gestational thrombocytopaenia most commonly present?
column2: Beyond 28 weeks gestation (it rarely presents in the first trimester).

column1: Under 12 weeks gestation, what specific clinical events indicate anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis in Rhesus D-negative women?
column2: Ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy, therapeutic termination of pregnancy, or repeated/heavy/painful uterine bleeding.

column1: What is the minimum recommended dose of anti-D immunoglobulin for sensitizing events occurring before 20 weeks gestation?
column2: $250\text{ IU}$ (administered within 72 hours of the event).

column1: Is a test for feto-maternal haemorrhage required following a sensitizing event before 20 weeks gestation?
column2: No, a test for feto-maternal haemorrhage is not required for events under 20 weeks gestation.

column1: What routine gestational age schedules are recommended for prophylactic anti-D administration in Rhesus D-negative women?
column2: Either a single large dose at 28 weeks gestation, or two doses given at 28 and 34 weeks gestation.

column1: Under what condition is anti-D immunoglobulin administered to a Rhesus D-negative woman in the postpartum period?
column2: When testing of umbilical cord blood confirms that the neonate is Rhesus D positive.

column1: Which non-invasive screening technique on maternal blood can determine fetal Rhesus status to avoid unnecessary anti-D prophylaxis?
column2: Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) analyzing cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA).

column1: What initial screening tools are used at the booking visit to assess a pregnant woman's risk for thalassaemia?
column2: The Family Origin Questionnaire (FOQ) and full blood count (FBC) results.

column1: What pattern of genetic inheritance characterizes thalassaemia and sickle cell disorders?
column2: Autosomal recessive pattern.

column1: Within what time frame following a potentially sensitizing event must anti-D immunoglobulin be administered?
column2: As soon as possible, and always within 72 hours of the event.

column1: Why is repeat blood group and antibody screening recommended for all pregnant women at 28 weeks gestation?
column2: To identify atypical maternal red cell antibodies that require clinical monitoring and to confirm Rhesus D status prior to prophylaxis.

column1: What dietary recommendation regarding starchy foods should be given to pregnant women during antenatal counseling?
column2: Choose whole grain varieties of starchy foods (e.g., whole grain bread, brown rice, whole wheat pasta).

column1: Which exercise activities are explicitly safe and encouraged for maintenance during uncomplicated pregnancy?
column2: Aerobic conditioning, strength exercises, walking, swimming, non-contact exercise, and pelvic floor exercises.

column1: What key long-term health benefit does breastfeeding provide for the child later in life?
column2: Reduced risk of obesity later in life and association with a higher intelligence quotient (IQ).

column1: What key parameter is routinely screened in urine during return antenatal visits?
column2: Proteinuria (protein in urine).

column1: What is the clinical definition of induction of labour?
column2: Stimulating the uterus to begin labour.

column1: What is the clinical definition of augmentation of labour?
column2: Stimulating the uterus during active labour to increase the frequency, duration, and strength of contractions.

column1: What contraction frequency and duration define an established good labour pattern?
column2: Three contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting more than 40 seconds.

column1: What are five recognized clinical indications for the induction of labour?
column2: Post-dates pregnancy, SGA/IUGR, pre-eclampsia, spontaneous/premature rupture of membranes (PROM), and antepartum haemorrhage (abruptio placentae).

column1: What is the recommended interval before repeating induction of labour with a mechanical method after an initial failed attempt?
column2: 48 hours

column1: What management is indicated if induction of labour fails and repeated induction is inappropriate or unacceptable?
column2: Caesarean section (CS)

column1: What is the most common underlying cause of primary dysfunctional labour (PDL)?
column2: Inadequate uterine activity.

column1: Besides primary dysfunctional labour and prolonged latent phase, what pattern characterizes abnormal progress of labour?
column2: Secondary arrest of cervical dilatation.

column1: What graphic recording tool allows visual assessment of cervical dilatation progress compared to expected norms by parity?
column2: The partogram

column1: How frequently should fetal heart rate (FHR) be auscultated during the first stage of intrapartum labour?
column2: Every 15 minutes.

column1: How frequently should fetal heart rate (FHR) be auscultated during the second stage of intrapartum labour?
column2: At least every 5 minutes.

column1: When performing intermittent auscultation during labour, for how long and at what point in the contraction cycle must the fetal heart rate be assessed?
column2: For at least 1 minute, immediately after a uterine contraction.

column1: What is the current guideline recommendation regarding routine 'admission cardiotocography (CTG)' for all labouring women?
column2: Routine admission CTG on all women is no longer recommended.

column1: What is the recommended standard time interval for performing routine vaginal examinations during the first stage of labour?
column2: Every 4 hours (or as clinically indicated).

column1: Why are adequate hydration and a light diet maintained during the first stage of intrapartum labour?
column2: To prevent maternal ketosis.

column1: What is the recommended mode of delivery for most laboring women in the absence of absolute contraindications?
column2: Vaginal birth

column1: How is Heavy Menstrual Bleeding (HMB) defined?
column2: Excessive menstrual blood loss interfering with a woman's physical, social, emotional, and/or material quality of life.

column1: What benign structural uterine and cervical lesions are commonly associated with Inter-menstrual Bleeding (IMB)?
column2: Endometrial polyps, cervical polyps, and endometriosis.

column1: Post-coital bleeding (PCB) is bleeding after intercourse. Which anatomical organ pathology is most commonly implicated?
column2: Cervical abnormalities (e.g., cervical ectropion, polyps, or cervical neoplasia).

column1: How is Post-menopausal Bleeding (PMB) defined, and what diagnostic priority must be addressed?
column2: Bleeding occurring $>1\text{ year}$ after cessation of periods; endometrial pathology (malignancy) or vaginal atrophy must be evaluated.

column1: What structural etiology categories are represented by the 'PALM' acronym in the FIGO classification of abnormal uterine bleeding?
column2: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy and hyperplasia.

column1: What non-structural etiology categories are represented by the 'COEIN' acronym in the FIGO classification of abnormal uterine bleeding?
column2: Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified.

column1: What are the typical age ranges for the physiological onset of Menarche and the establishment of Menopause?
column2: Menarche: 11--14 years; Menopause: 45--55 years.

column1: What defines Primary Dysmenorrhoea, and how does its natural course change with age and parity?
column2: Painful menstruation since menarche without identifiable underlying pathology; typically improves after childbirth and declines with increasing age.

column1: What defines Secondary Dysmenorrhoea?
column2: Painful menstruation secondary to underlying pelvic pathology (e.g., endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, PID).

column1: What estimated percentage of postpubertal girls experience dysmenorrhoea?
column2: Up to 50%

column1: What first-line dietary and lifestyle modifications are recommended for managing mild-to-moderate premenstrual syndrome (PMS)?
column2: Reduce fat, sugar, salt, caffeine, and alcohol; consume frequent high-fibre starchy meals, fruits, and vegetables; engage in regular exercise and stress management.

column1: What validated symptom chart/diary is used to prospectusly record daily symptoms and assess treatment response in PMS?
column2: Daily Record of Severity of Problems (DRSP)

column1: Which specialist referral is indicated for women presenting with severe PMS combined with marked underlying psychopathology?
column2: Referral to a psychiatrist.

column1: At what age is formal investigation of primary amenorrhoea indicated in the presence of normal secondary sexual development?
column2: Age 16

column1: At what age is formal investigation of primary amenorrhoea indicated when secondary sexual characteristics are absent?
column2: Age 14

column1: What age threshold defines Premature Ovarian Failure?
column2: Cessation of menses before 40 years of age.

column1: What common ovarian endocrine disorder leads to anovulatory secondary amenorrhoea?
column2: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)

column1: What structural pathology causes Asherman syndrome, and what type of amenorrhoea does it produce?
column2: Intrauterine adhesions (synechiae) and endometrial scarring causing secondary amenorrhoea. Diagram comparing normal uterine cavity with intrauterine synechiae in Asherman's syndrome

column1: What classic uterine surgical procedure post-delivery or post-miscarriage is the primary iatrogenic cause of Asherman syndrome?
column2: Dilatation and Curettage (D&C)

column1: Which structural developmental defects present as primary amenorrhoea with outflow tract obstruction and haematocolpos?
column2: Müllerian duct anomalies (e.g., imperforate hymen or transverse vaginal septum).

column1: What management strategy is indicated for functional secondary amenorrhoea caused by abnormally low body weight (low BMI)?
column2: Dietary advice, nutritional support, and weight restoration.

column1: What is the mathematical formula for calculating the Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) in post-menopausal women with ovarian cysts?
column2: $\text{RMI} = U \times M \times \text{CA-125}$ where $U$ is Ultrasound score, $M$ is Menopausal status, and $\text{CA-125}$ is serum CA-125 level (U/mL).

column1: What Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) score threshold warrants immediate referral to a specialist gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team?
column2: $\text{RMI} > 200$

column1: Calculate the RMI of a post-menopausal woman ($M = 3$) with a serum CA-125 level of $15\text{ U/mL}$ and ultrasound features of a multiloculated bilateral cyst ($U = 3$).
column2: $\text{RMI} = 3 \times 3 \times 15 = 135$

column1: Which three clinical factors comprise the triad used in RCOG triage for ovarian cyst malignancy risk assessment?
column2: Ultrasound score ($U$), Menopausal status ($M$), and Serum CA-125 level.

column1: According to FIGO staging for ovarian carcinoma, what defining anatomical scope characterizes Stage II disease?
column2: Tumour involves one or both ovaries with pelvic extension (below the pelvic brim) or primary peritoneal cancer.

column1: How is FIGO Stage IIA differentiated from Stage IIB in ovarian cancer staging?
column2: Stage IIA involves extension to/implants on the uterus and/or fallopian tubes; Stage IIB involves extension to other pelvic intraperitoneal tissues.

column1: What investigation is performed postmortem or post-delivery to confirm feto-maternal haemorrhage in RhD-negative women following an intrauterine fetal death (IUFD)?
column2: Kleihauer-Betke test

column1: What maternal blood screening component is indicated in the maternal diagnostic workup following an unexplained IUFD or severe IUGR?
column2: Maternal thrombophilia screening (and TORCH/Syphilis serology).

column1: What parental laboratory investigation is indicated following intrauterine fetal death (IUFD) to identify structural genetic causes?
column2: Parental blood for karyotyping.

column1: What non-pharmacological supportive measure during the first stage of labour promotes physiological progress and pain control?
column2: One-to-one continuous midwifery care and emotional support from a dedicated birth partner.

column1: Which single-gene autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathy alters haemoglobin structure and is widely screened at booking?
column2: Sickle cell disease (HbSS, HbSC, HbS-beta thalassaemia).

column1: Why is rubella immunity status assessed during antenatal care screening?
column2: To identify susceptible non-immune women so post-partum MMR vaccination can be offered to protect future pregnancies.

column1: What is the key clinical objective of antenatal care regarding minor ailments of pregnancy?
column2: To deal with minor ailments and provide reassurance, advice, education, and support to the woman and her family.

column1: When evaluating uterine contractions during labour, what three parameters are monitored to assess contraction quality?
column2: Frequency, duration, and strength of contractions.

column1: What diagnostic finding at staging laparotomy places an ovarian malignancy involving the left ovary and uterus with positive peritoneal washings into FIGO Stage IIA?
column2: Direct extension or metastases strictly to the uterus and/or fallopian tubes (Stage IIA).
